entries.meaning: The grief-filled words exchanged as the two kings met formed river currents that submerged the banks of knowledge and detachment. Sighs and sorrow were the wind and waves, breaking the trees of courage upon the shore. A difficult torrent of despondency cut the channel; fear and delusion were endless whirlpools and eddies. Though understanding and learning were able ferrymen with a great boat, they could not row and no one knew how to cross. The poor forest-dwelling Kols and Kirātas watched until, exhausted, they too lost heart. When the river finally met the ocean of the hermitage, that ocean seemed to rise in anguish. Both royal companies became overwhelmed with grief; knowledge, courage, and modesty remained no more. Praising Daśaratha’s form, virtues, and character, they plunged into the ocean of sorrow and wept.

Janaka’s wisdom was a sun that destroys the night of becoming and whose verbal rays cause sage-lotuses to bloom—how could delusion and attachment approach him? His condition only magnified his love for Sītā and Rāma. The Vedas describe three kinds of worldly people: sense-bound, practitioners, and accomplished wise ones; in an assembly of saints, the greatest honor belongs to the one whose heart is moistened by love for Rāma. Knowledge without that love does not shine, as a watercraft without a helmsman cannot. Sages consoled Videha in many ways, and everyone bathed at Rāmaghāṭa. Men and women spent that entire day crowded with sorrow and without water; even animals and birds took no food—what need to speak of beloved family? At dawn the two companies of Janaka and Raghurāja bathed, then sat beneath the banyan with minds dejected and bodies lean.

The learned brahmins who lived in Daśaratha’s city, and those of the lord of Mithilā’s city, began teaching. Janaka’s family priest and guru, born in the lineage of the swanlike sage Śatānanda, had explored the world’s path and the highest good; with duty, policy, detachment, and discernment, they delivered many instructions. Viśvāmitra repeatedly related ancient narratives and used gracious speech to console the assembly. Raghunātha then told him: ‘Lord, yesterday everyone remained without water.’ The sage agreed that Rāma spoke rightly; two and a half watches of the day had passed. Reading the sages’ inclination, the king of Tirhut said that grain-food was not fitting there. Everyone approved the king’s words, received permission, and went to bathe. At that moment forest dwellers arrived carrying many loads in shoulder-yokes filled with abundant varieties of leaves, flowers, fruit, and roots.

By Rāma’s grace, the wish-granting mountain destroys sorrow as soon as one sees it. Ponds, rivers, forests, and regions of land seemed to overflow with joy and love; every vine and tree bore fruit and flowers, while birds, animals, and bees called favorably. The forest’s delight grew especially at that time, and three kinds of pleasant breeze comforted everyone. Its charm was indescribable, as though earth herself were extending hospitality to Janaka. Everyone bathed again and again with the permission of Rāma, Janaka, and the sages. Gazing lovingly at the fine trees, citizens began lodging here and there. Leaves, fruit, roots, and tubers of many sorts were sacred, beautiful, and like nectar. Rāma’s guru respectfully sent everyone load after load. After worshiping ancestors, gods, guests, and guru, all began their fruit diet.

Four days passed in this way, and men and women found happiness in gazing upon Rāma. Both companies cherished the same desire: returning without Sītā and Rāma would not be good. Exile in the forest with Sītā and Rāma seemed equal to millions of celestial cities; whoever preferred a home after abandoning Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma, and Vaidehī had hostile destiny. If fate turned favorable for everyone, they would live in the forest close to Rāma, bathe three times daily in the Mandākinī, and behold Rāma, a garland of joy and blessing. Wandering Rāma’s mountain, forest, and ascetic places and eating nectar-like roots and fruit, even twenty-seven happy years would pass like a moment without being noticed. ‘People are not worthy of such happiness,’ they said; ‘where could one gain such fortune?’ Both companies were naturally attached to Rāma’s feet.

Everyone formed hopes in this way, and their loving words delighted the heart. At that time Sītā’s mother sent maidservants, who arrived after noticing a good opportunity. Hearing there was leisure, all Sītā’s mothers-in-law came, and Janaka’s queen arrived with the women of her palace. Kausalyā honored them respectfully and offered seats suited to the occasion. Seeing and hearing the gracious love on both sides would have melted even thunderbolt-hard hearts. Bodies thrilled and slackened, eyes filled with water, and every woman traced the earth with her nails, lost in thought. Each seemed an image of Sītā and Rāma’s love, as though compassion mourned in many forms. Sītā’s mother said: ‘Destiny’s intelligence is crooked: it pierces milk-foam with a thunderbolt and cuts rock with a blade of grass. One hears nectar and sees poison in all its dreadful acts; everywhere there are crows, owls, and cranes, but upon Lake Mānasa only one swan.’

Hearing Sunayanā, Queen Sumitrā sorrowfully said: ‘Destiny’s course is exceedingly contrary and strange: it creates, sustains, and then destroys, its foolish purpose like a child’s game.’ Kausalyā replied: ‘No one is at fault; bound by action, beings receive pain and pleasure, loss and gain. Only the Creator knows action’s difficult course and gives all auspicious and inauspicious fruits. The Lord’s command rests upon every head—creation, continuance, dissolution, poison, and nectar. Queen, grieving from delusion is futile; destiny’s web is eternally established and beginningless. Bringing the king’s living or dying into the heart, we should grieve only when we see harm to our true good.’ Sītā’s mother praised her truthful speech and called the queen of Ayodhyā blessed in merit. ‘It is well that Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma, and Sītā go to the forest; the outcome is not evil.’ Her heart choking, Kausalyā said: ‘My concern is for Bharata.’

Kausalyā continued: ‘Through the Lord’s grace and your blessing, my sons and daughter-in-law are like water of the celestial river. By Rāma’s oath, friend, I have never sworn falsely; invoking it now, I speak my true feeling. Bharata’s conduct, virtues, humility, greatness, brotherly devotion, trustworthiness, and goodness would humble even Sarasvatī’s understanding if she tried to tell them—can a shell empty the ocean? I have always known Bharata as the lamp of the dynasty; the king told me so again and again. Gold is tested upon the touchstone and a jewel by the appraiser; a person’s nature is tested in time of trial. For me to say this today is improper, for grief and affection have reduced my wisdom.’ Hearing speech sacred as the Gaṅgā, all the queens were overwhelmed by love. Gathering courage, Kausalyā told the queen of Mithilā: ‘Who can instruct you, a treasury of discernment and beloved of Janaka?’

Kausalyā asked Sunayanā: ‘When you find an opportunity, explain the matter to the king in your own way. Let Lakṣmaṇa be kept here and Bharata go to the forest, if the king’s mind accepts this judgment. Then, after careful thought, make that good arrangement. My concern for Bharata is very heavy. With such profound love hidden in his heart, his remaining here does not seem good to me.’ Observing her nature and hearing the simple words, all the queens became submerged in compassion. Flowers fell from heaven amid cries of ‘Blessed!’ Even accomplished yogins and sages weakened with affection. The whole women’s assembly sat stunned. Sumitrā then steadied herself and said: ‘Queen, two watches of night have passed.’ Rāma’s mother heard, rose lovingly, and urged Sunayanā in genuine affection: ‘Please go quickly to your place. Our only course now rests with the Lord, and the lord of Mithilā is our ally.’

Seeing Kausalyā’s love and hearing her humble words, Janaka’s beloved clasped her sacred feet: ‘Queen, your request is entirely fitting—you are Daśaratha’s wife and Rāma’s mother. The Lord honors even the lowly; fire bears smoke upward and mountains carry grass upon their heads. In deed, mind, and speech the king is your servant, and Maheśa and Bhavānī are always your helpers. Who in the world is worthy to act as your limb? Does a lamp assist the sun in shining? Rāma has gone to the forest to accomplish the gods’ purpose and will afterward rule immovably in Ayodhyā. Gods, Nāgas, and humans will dwell happily in their own places through Rāma’s arm-strength. Yājñavalkya has already told all this; a sage’s speech does not prove vain.’ With profound love she bowed at Kausalyā’s feet and submitted her concern for Sītā; then, receiving gracious permission, Sītā’s mother departed with Sītā.
